clue.text: I'm galvanised, excited — and short of twenty

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up, so the letters of I'm galvanised are jumbled
short means lacking, so the letters of the word and are left out of the jumble

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled by an electric jolt confesses they are just shy of their twentieth birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: A subtractive anagram: 'excited' scrambles I'M GALVANISED, and 'short' says the A, N and D of 'and' are missing from the result, leaving nine letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Vigesimal is the adjective for counting in scores, so it describes things based on or relating to the number twenty.

clue.text: Six wheels are incumbent

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
wheels is slang for a car

explanation.surface: Someone notes that half a dozen wheels are obligatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incumbent' looks like an adjective meaning obligatory, but it is a noun: the holder of a church living.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Church of England the incumbent of a parish is its priest, often a vicar.

clue.text: If you want a cup of tea — run down

definitions.text: If you want a cup of tea
definitions.meaning: a playful sense: to get tea you head off to the teapot
to run down is to deteriorate or fall into ruin

explanation.definitionFit: Literally one heads for the teapot for a brew; idiomatically, going to pot means falling into decay.

clue.text: Liberals fall out with me; I left, but that's unimportant

indicators.note: fall out suggests a quarrel breaking up the group, so the letters of the words are rearranged
I left means the letter I departs from the jumbled letters

explanation.surface: A politician quits after a row with the Liberals, insisting it was a trivial matter.
explanation.walkthrough: A subtractive anagram: 'fall out' scrambles LIBERALS plus ME, and 'I left' removes one I from those ten letters. 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Small beer is weak beer, and by extension something trivial or of little consequence.

clue.text: Young lady, given the gravy jug, can't grab it quick enough

parts.note: miss is the title for a young unmarried woman
taken as written
a gravy boat is the jug in which gravy is served

explanation.surface: A girl handed the gravy at dinner fumbles it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given' is a link word. 'gravy jug' gives BOAT, from gravy boat.
explanation.definitionFit: To miss the boat is an idiom for failing to take an opportunity in time.

clue.text: 100,000 insects secrete this

definitions.meaning: in South Asia a lakh, also spelt this way, is one hundred thousand
a resin produced by ... insects, used for shellac

explanation.definitionFit: The Indian number word for a hundred thousand shares its spelling with the resin secreted by scale insects.

clue.text: "It's a grind," beau said

indicators.note: said tells us the word is spoken, so we want a spelling that sounds like the dandy's surname

parts.note: Beau Nash was the celebrated eighteenth-century dandy and master of ceremonies at Bath

explanation.surface: A dandy, asked about some tedious chore, complains that it is a slog.
explanation.walkthrough: Beau Nash, the famous Georgian dandy who ran society in Bath, England, supplies the surname; the silent G of the answer leaves the sound unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: To gnash is to grind the teeth together, so the clue's grind is the motion meant.

clue.text: Eat too much, and drink up last of wine

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the drink word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: grog is a drink, originally rum and water

indicators.note: last of points to the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Someone overeats and then finishes off the last of the wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drink up' reads as a phrase, but 'up' reverses GROG to give GORG.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to stuff oneself greedily with food.

clue.text: Firm's advertisement attracting a male worker

parts.note: taken as written
an ant is the classic worker in crosswords

explanation.surface: A company's job advert is drawing in a male employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company, but it is the definition, an adjective; the 's means is. 'attracting' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant means unshakeable or resolute, refusing to be persuaded.

clue.text: Polish and do up snare

parts.note: to hone is to sharpen or polish

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for a do is written from bottom to top

parts.note: a do is a party or social event

explanation.surface: Someone is told to tidy and decorate in time for a hunter's trap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is a link. 'do up' reads as decorate, but 'do' is a party and 'up' turns it round in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A honeytrap is a scheme to snare someone, often by seduction.

clue.text: Refined, but not grand, weapon

indicators.note: not tells us one element is to be dropped from the longer word for refined

parts.note: a cut-glass accent is a refined, upper-class one
G is the standard abbreviation for grand, slang for a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A sword is described as elegant but rather modest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' is only a link here. Take CUT-GLASS, the British term for a very refined, posh accent, and drop the G.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutlass is a short, broad, slightly curved sword once favoured by sailors.

clue.text: Short answer —- batting or hanging?

parts.note: curt means short or brusque in manner
in cricket the side batting is said to be in

explanation.surface: A cricket spectator asks tersely whether a player is at the crease or about to be dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the side batting is 'in'. 'hanging' looks like part of the cricket question, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A curtain is a length of fabric hung at a window or stage, a hanging in the furnishing sense.

clue.text: Abrogation, not a revolt

indicators.note: not a means the single letter A is dropped from the word for abrogation

parts.note: abrogation is the formal cancelling of a law, which is a repeal

explanation.surface: A legal commentator insists that cancelling a law is not the same as an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolt' reads as the noun for an uprising, but it is the verb meaning to disgust.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel is to disgust or sicken someone, which is what revolting a person means.

clue.text: Someone dumping rubbish by a railway —- it's a long way away

parts.note: a tipper is a person who tips, or dumps, waste
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fly-tipper is spotted leaving waste beside a remote railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls the First World War song 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary'; Tipperary is a town and county in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The marching song famously sang of the Irish town as a long, long distance off.

clue.text: A flyer of Mona Lisa, perhaps

definitions.meaning: the famous portrait shows a woman rendered in paint

explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a common orange butterfly, and Leonardo's portrait is literally a woman in paint.

clue.text: Stop to refuel where orchestra plays

definitions.meaning: in motor racing a car stops in the ... for fuel, and to ... is to make that stop
a theatre's orchestra plays in the sunken area in front of the stage

explanation.definitionFit: A racing driver pits for fuel and tyres, and an opera orchestra sits in the sunken area below the stage.

clue.text: Produced music sheets for "Pie in the sky"

parts.note: piped means played on a pipe, producing music
a ream is a quantity of sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Someone printed sheet music for a song called 'Pie in the Sky'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. Pie in the sky is an idiom for an unrealistic hope.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe a fanciful hope that is never likely to come true.

clue.text: Given a stern struggle, one of 28?

indicators.note: struggle suggests writhing and twisting, so the letters of the phrase are tangled up

explanation.surface: Someone faces a tough fight from the back of a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one of 28' points to the answer at 28 across, SKYLIGHTS, playfully read as lights in the sky; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus seen at dusk is a bright light in the sky, so it counts as a skylight in the playful sense.

clue.text: Soldier devouring a blue biscuit

indicators.note: devouring means the soldier swallows the other pieces, holding them inside

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
taken as written
blue means risqué or smutty, as is ribald

explanation.surface: A soldier is wolfing down an indecent cookie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' means risqué, not a colour. A garibaldi is a British biscuit with a layer of squashed currants.
explanation.definitionFit: A garibaldi is a flat British currant biscuit named after the Italian patriot.

clue.text: Lift toes, partner, when dancing

indicators.note: dancing suggests feet moving about, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dance instructor tells a couple to raise their toes as they move together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' looks like an instruction to the dancers, but it is the definition: a paternoster is a lift of open cars on a continuous loop. 'when' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A paternoster is a type of elevator with doorless compartments moving continuously in a loop, still found in some old European buildings.

clue.text: Not like fanciful writer

indicators.note: fanciful suggests something freely imagined, so the letters of the phrase are reworked

explanation.surface: An imaginative author is described as nothing like others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fanciful' looks like a description of the writer, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: J R R Tolkien was the English author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

clue.text: Roll baked and prepared for starters

indicators.note: for starters points to the opening letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A bread roll has been baked and made ready for the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: A bap is a soft, round British bread roll.
explanation.definitionFit: A bap is a soft, flattish bread bun, the sort of roll used for a bacon sandwich.

clue.text: Nationality of little brother established at length

clue.text: An achievement, to obscure luminescence over the moon

indicators.note: to obscure something is to hide it by wrapping around it, so the achievement word goes round the glow

parts.note: a deed is an achievement or feat
luminescence is light given off

explanation.surface: An astronomer's feat is to block the moonlight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over the moon' looks like part of the astronomy, but it is the definition: an idiom for very happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the moon is a British idiom for thrilled or overjoyed.

clue.text: Blood all round scratch initially produced by this prickly shrub

indicators.note: all round means the blood word encircles the next piece

parts.note: gore is blood, especially shed blood

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A gardener's arm is bloodied all over by a scratch from a thorny bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced by this' is a link phrase joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorse, also called furze, is a spiny yellow-flowered shrub of heaths.

clue.text: Colonel returns one pound to provost

indicators.note: returns means the pair of pieces for one and pound is read backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
LB is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
a provost marshal heads the military police, the MP

explanation.surface: An army colonel hands back a single pound to a college or civic official.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Blimp is a pompous, reactionary cartoon officer from 1930s British newspapers. A provost is a military police officer, giving MP.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Blimp was David Low's cartoon character, a byword for a pompous, reactionary old officer.

clue.text: Journalists insist on jam roll

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Journalists insist on jam roll', gives journalists, insist on and jam as senses, but 'roll' has no job found; the down clues are missing from the scan and no search found the clue.

clue.text: Gnome looks good in the border when it's turned around

indicators.note: in means the word for good sits inside the other piece
turned around means the word for border is read from right to left

parts.note: marge is an old poetic word for a margin or border
pi, short for pious, is crossword shorthand for good

explanation.surface: A garden gnome looks smart standing in the flower bed after being turned to face the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' is not a garden ornament but a pithy saying. 'looks' and 'the' are link words; marge is an archaic word for a margin.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnome in this sense is a short pithy maxim, as is an epigram.

clue.text: Count up characters here

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for count is written from bottom to top

parts.note: to sum is to count up or add

explanation.surface: Someone is told to tally the letters in this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Mu is the Greek letter M; 'here' is a link pointing at the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, and letters are characters.

clue.text: Best yet: officer hiding in a tree!

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: hiding in means the officer is concealed inside the other pieces

parts.note: a lime is a linden tree
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant, an officer

explanation.surface: An excited report that an army officer has been found up a tree, a record achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best yet' reads as an exclamation, but it is the definition; the lime here is the linden tree, not the citrus fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-time record is the best ever achieved, unsurpassed up to now.

clue.text: Chap's energy goes into building

parts.note: a chap is a man, and the possessive gives man's
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A man pours all his energy into a construction project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes into' just joins the pieces. A manse is the house of a minister, especially in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A manse is the house provided for a Presbyterian or other Nonconformist minister.

clue.text: Windows giving views across channel that's been cut

indicators.note: across means the views word stretches over and around the channel word

parts.note: sights are things seen, views

indicators.note: cut means the channel word loses its last letter

parts.note: a kyle is a narrow sea channel or strait in Scotland, as in the Kyle of Lochalsh

explanation.surface: Windows offering views over a canal that has been dug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'channel' suggests a TV station or the English Channel; here it is a Scottish sea strait, a kyle, and 'that's been cut' docks its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Skylights are windows set into a roof or ceiling.
